## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.75889.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.75889.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "IL-37 expression reduces acute and chronic neuroinflammation and rescues cognitive impairment in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Jeannie Chin as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1. The expression profile of hIL-37 receptors on different cell types under different conditions should be shown. The phenotype seen in microglia in vitro was attributed to hIL-37 acting on microglia themselves, but it is not clear this is the only possibility.

2. Experiments using human cell lines or patient samples would provide additional validation.

3. The authors mentioned that in acute inflammation, little LPS is likely to enter the brain because of an intact blood-brain barrier (BBB). It is also possible that the peripherally-induced inflammation may contribute to the neuroinflammation centrally. Due to the systemic overexpression of hIL-37, to exclude the peripheral effects of hIL-37, the experiments of direct injection of hIL-37 into the brain would help clarify the conclusion.

4. Background, Lines 87,88: The overall premise that anti-inflammatory therapies will be beneficial in AD is overly simplistic. The inflammatory activation of glial cells is required as a protective immune response, including pro-inflammatory activation. Also, retrospective studies that have demonstrated that NSAIDs are not a successful therapeutic strategy go against this notion. Please consider rephrasing.

5. What is known about IL-37 expression in humans? Since it is expressed by all cells in the current model, will this hamper biological interpretation, since the brain RNAseq database suggests that it is highly enriched specifically in microglia? This confounding factor makes biological interpretation of the in-vivo data a little difficult.

6. Results, Page 4, Lines 148-152: Description of Figure 1C-1E is confusing and unclear as written. Please consider rephrasing.

7. Results, Page 5: The points about the TCA cycle metabolites is raised in this section for the first time. Please consider introducing this concept in relation to AD / related immune responses in the introduction.

8. Figure 3C: Please include what the X-axis is plotting? As a supplemental figure, please include your initial gating strategy used for all flow cytometry data. Are there any CD68+CD11b+ CD45 high cells in these animals? If an effect of IL-37 is seen in filtration of peripheral inflammatory macrophages into the brain, this is a very strong data set to improve the impact of this figure.

9. Results, page 7: The authors make the statement that IL-37 signaling has a significant impact on the pro-inflammatory activation of microglia in the brain. However, this is based on just the measurement of IL-1b and microglial numbers. The authors should measure other markers of inflammation that are known to go up in the brain upon LPS challenge. Maybe using an Elisa based multiplex assay such as MSD or Luminex to measure brain inflammatory cytokines will add to this data set.

10. Results, page 7: Figure 4A-4B: Was the LPS injection used for these experiments the same as outlined for figure 3? Please clarify this in the method section, especially since 2 different LPS treatment paradigms have been used for 4A-4B and 4G-4H.

11. The paradigm for the Y-maze testing (pre-treatment with IL-37, followed by IL1b), though in-line with the current study, is not biologically relevant. Since IL-37 will be upregulated as part of the neuroinflammatory response, have the authors tried to treat animals with IL-37 after IL-1b or concurrently with IL-1B?

12. Figure 1B: This figure suggests that 1 i.p injection with rIL-1B completely abolishes any working memory In WT mice. This is surprising. Please clarify.

13. For Figures6 and 7: Were both sexes used for APPPS1 studies? If so, please clarify in the methods section as to the number of males and females, given that female APPPS1 mice show more aggressive disease as compared to males.

14. Figure 6. Please show all gating strategies as well as relevant gates drawn to identify CD11b+ CD45low microglia, as well as the methoxy X-04+ vs methoxy X-04- microglia. Is there a CD11b+ CD45high microglial subset at this age, since at earlier timepoints, these distinct microglial subsets are evident and have different activation profiles.

15. Please include details of how brain tissue was processed to prepare single-cell suspension for all FACS data. i.e: percoll based density gradients or myelin removal beads etc?

16. Authors discuss their methoxy-X04 data as indicative of "increased clearance" of plaques. Careful interpretation of this data set is required as this assay only measures Abeta "uptake". Since no measures of clearance have been assessed, please reword and/ reinterpret this in the results and Discussion section.

17. Please include representative images for plaque loads in the cortex that correlate with quantification in 6I. Also, please include a representative image for differences in plaque size.

18. Figure 7A: Please mention the average age of the animals used in the 3 animal groups for MW testing. 9-12 months is a big age range for these animals and results will be skewed if one cohort is largely composed of older animals vs. younger.

19. The Discussion section is rather long and largely used to re-summarize results. The authors should reconsider using this section to put their data into context for the big-picture field of neurodegeneration. Some suggestions – How do the authors picture IL-37 signaling to play a role in human AD?

a. Given the detailed description of distinct microglial subsets associated with amyloid vs. tau pathology in AD, do the authors anticipate IL-37 to have distinct effects depending on pathological outcomes?

b. Literature has demonstrated that IL-1b, IL-6 and TNFa from reactive microglia may play a role in exacerbating tau-spread. The authors should discuss the implications of their findings in this light

c. Is anything is known about IL-37 signaling in other neuroinflammatory models (injury, MS etc)? A possible discussion of these in the context of neuroprotection may strengthen this section.

20. in vitro phenotypes in Figure 1 were not closely connected with the following in vivo neuroinflammation phenotypes. Although three different neuroinflammation models were used, the detailed mechanisms for how IL-37 reduced neuroinflammation were not well addressed.

21) Figure 3 and Figure 5 showed reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production in brain lysates. However, glial cells other than microglia, such as astrocytes and infiltrating leukocytes could be sources of inflammatory cytokines. There was no evidence supporting that reduced cytokine levels were intrinsic to microglia as modelled in the in vitro system. Thus, in vitro and in vivo phenotypes appeared somewhat disconnected.

22) In Figure 5, IL-1β-induced neuroinflammation model was used to demonstrate the beneficial effects of IL-37 on cognition and synaptic function. Could injection of recombinant IL-37 display similar effects for LPS challenge model in Figure 3 and Figure 4?

23) Reduced IL-37-mediated neuroinflammation was shown in both chronic and acute models in the manuscript. Did microglia or other cells play a major role in those models? The detailed mechanisms regarding cell type contribution were largely missing in the manuscript.

24. Figure 2 showed differential metabolomic profiling of microglial cells between WT and IL-37tg mice. However, there was no further evidence demonstrating that the metabolic function of microglial cells was indeed altered by IL-37 expression. It would be better to show the results of seahorse or other metabolic functional assays.

25. The models for acute neuroinflammation including LPS and IL-1β challenge were systematic inflammation. It might be reasonable to propose that reduced neuroinflammation was a secondary effect to reduced inflammation response in the periphery. In addition, in Figure 3, would injection of LPS twice induce tolerance responses?

26. In Figure 3 and Figure 6, CD68 was used as an activation marker for microglia. However, CD68 expression by itself is not enough to define microglia to be in the activation state. The phenotypic changes of microglial cells would also depend on specific models used. Additional experimental evidence is needed for defining the reduced activation status of microglia in IL-37tg mice.

results.result: Primary microglial cells from IL-37 transgenic mice exhibit reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β) after LPS stimulation in vitro, with LPS inducing increased IL-37 mRNA expression in transgenic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 provide converging evidence from dose-response experiments, time-course analyses, and multiple cytokine measurements with appropriate statistical tests (ANOVA, t-tests) and clear p-values. The data demonstrate consistent anti-inflammatory effects of IL-37 expression in primary microglia across different LPS concentrations and time points, supported by Figure 1B-G.

results.result: Primary astrocytes from IL-37tg mice did not show reduced inflammatory cytokine levels after LPS stimulation, suggesting cell-type specificity of IL-37 effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 provides important negative control data showing that IL-37's anti-inflammatory effects are specific to microglia and not observed in astrocytes, strengthening the conclusion about microglial-specific signaling. This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

results.result: Recombinant IL-37 pretreatment reduces LPS-induced IL-6 release in wild-type primary microglial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 demonstrate that exogenous IL-37 can recapitulate the anti-inflammatory effects observed in transgenic cells, with appropriate dose-response data (100 ng/mL and 500 ng/mL) and statistical analysis (ANOVA with p-values). This is supported by Figure 1H.

results.result: IL-37 expression in microglial cells attenuates LPS-induced pro-inflammatory metabolic reprogramming, specifically reducing levels of itaconate and succinate.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 provide metabolomic evidence with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001) showing that IL-37 limits metabolic changes associated with inflammation. The data are supported by Figure 2A-C and include proper controls and multiple metabolite measurements.

results.result: Systemic LPS administration induces microglial activation and neuroinflammation in wild-type mice (increased CD68+ cells, IL-1β levels, IBA-1+ cell numbers), which is prevented in IL-37tg mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 provide comprehensive in vivo evidence using multiple complementary methods (FACS, ELISA, immunohistochemistry) with appropriate statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA). The convergent evidence from different markers of microglial activation strongly supports the anti-inflammatory effect of IL-37 in vivo, as shown in Figures 3B-I.

results.result: Systemic LPS administration impairs hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP) and reduces dendritic spine density in wild-type mice, but these deficits are prevented in IL-37tg mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 demonstrate functional and structural neuronal consequences of neuroinflammation with appropriate electrophysiological measurements and morphological analyses. Statistical tests (two-way ANOVA) with clear p-values support the protective effects of IL-37 on synaptic plasticity and neuronal structure, as shown in Figures 4A-F.

results.result: Direct application of LPS to acute hippocampal slices impairs LTP in wild-type but not IL-37tg slices, demonstrating local CNS effects of IL-37 independent of peripheral immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide critical mechanistic evidence that IL-37 acts directly in the CNS rather than solely through peripheral immune modulation. The ex vivo slice experiments with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, p-values reported) support this conclusion, as shown in Figures 4G-I.

results.result: Recombinant IL-37 pretreatment protects wild-type mice from IL-1β-induced cognitive deficits in the Y-maze test and reduces brain levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1α).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 demonstrate therapeutic potential of recombinant IL-37 with behavioral and biochemical evidence. The Y-maze data show functional cognitive protection, and ELISA measurements confirm reduced neuroinflammation with appropriate statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA). This is supported by Figures 5B-D.

results.result: APP/PS1-IL37tg mice show reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-6, IL-1β) and decreased microglial activation (CD68+ cells) compared to APP/PS1 mice across multiple ages (6, 9-12, and 20-23 months).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 provide longitudinal evidence of IL-37's anti-inflammatory effects in a chronic neuroinflammation model with appropriate statistical analyses (one-way ANOVA, Bonferroni's post-hoc tests). The age-dependent analysis strengthens the conclusions about chronic effects, as shown in Figures 6B-G.

results.result: APP/PS1-IL37tg mice exhibit reduced amyloid-β plaque burden and size in hippocampus and cortex, with increased microglial phagocytosis of Aβ particles compared to APP/PS1 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 demonstrate that IL-37 affects AD pathology with quantitative plaque analysis (t-tests with p-values) and functional phagocytosis assays (FACS-based uptake measurements with ANOVA). The convergent evidence from plaque burden, size, and uptake studies strongly supports enhanced Aβ clearance, as shown in Figures 6H-M.

results.result: APP/PS1-IL37tg mice show improved spatial learning and memory in the Morris water maze compared to APP/PS1 mice, with rescued preference for the target quadrant in the probe trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide behavioral evidence of cognitive rescue with appropriate statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA for training, t-tests for probe trials). The escape latency data during training and target quadrant preference in probe trials demonstrate functional cognitive improvement, as shown in Figures 7B-D.

results.result: APP/PS1-IL37tg mice show rescued induction phase (but not maintenance phase) of hippocampal LTP compared to APP/PS1 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 demonstrate partial rescue of synaptic plasticity with appropriate electrophysiological measurements and statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA). The distinction between induction and maintenance phases is important for understanding the limitations of IL-37's effects, as shown in Figures 7E-G.

results.result: APP/PS1-IL37tg mice show preserved dendritic spine density in CA1 pyramidal neurons compared to APP/PS1 mice, which exhibit significant spine loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 provide morphological evidence of neuronal protection with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA). The spine density measurements complement the LTP data and support structural preservation of synapses, as shown in Figures 7H-I.

results.result: IL-37 expression plays a protective role against chronic neuroinflammation in the APP/PS1 mouse model by ameliorating learning and memory deficits and rescuing cellular correlates.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is a summary conclusion supported by the convergent evidence from claims C84-C101, including reduced inflammation, improved plaque clearance, rescued cognitive function, and preserved synaptic structure and function. This integrative conclusion is well-supported by the comprehensive dataset.

results.result: LPS challenge induces 11,014 differentially expressed genes in microglia from both WT and IL-37tg mice, with enrichment in interleukin-1 signaling pathways, but no significant overall differences between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 provide transcriptomic evidence with appropriate RNA-seq analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). While no significant differences were found between genotypes (important negative result), the massive transcriptional response to LPS is well-documented, as shown in Figures 8A-C.

results.result: Several inflammation-related genes (Saa2, Vgf, Bcl6b, Il23a, Icam1) show slightly reduced upregulation in IL-37tg microglia after LPS, while genes associated with neurological function (Tk2, Kcnj9, Kif21b) show attenuated downregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C114 identify specific genes with differential expression patterns between genotypes, though the differences are modest. The genes are appropriately cited and their biological relevance is established, providing mechanistic insights despite the lack of genome-wide significance, as shown in Figures 8D-K.

results.result: Several inflammation-related genes (Gpr84, Mmp3, Acod1) and the IL-18 receptor (Il18r) are equally upregulated in both WT and IL-37tg microglia after LPS challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 document genes that respond similarly in both genotypes, with Il18r upregulation suggesting a potential mechanism for IL-37 signaling. The data are appropriately presented with citations for gene functions, as shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D.

results.result: IL-37 reduces both acute and chronic neuroinflammation, and the IL-37tg mouse model is valuable for studying neurodegenerative diseases caused by chronic inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are overarching conclusions supported by the comprehensive dataset from both acute LPS and chronic APP/PS1 experiments. The evidence from multiple experimental paradigms, outcome measures, and time points strongly supports these summary statements.

results.result: IL-37 reduces inflammatory markers in CNS microglia but not in astrocytes, suggesting microglial-specific modulatory effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are supported by the in vitro data comparing microglia (C48-C55) and astrocytes (C56), demonstrating cell-type specificity. This conclusion is important for understanding the mechanism of IL-37 action in the CNS.

results.result: IL-37 reduces inflammation in microglial cells in vitro through its anti-inflammatory properties.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 is a summary conclusion well-supported by the in vitro data (C48-C63) showing reduced cytokine release and attenuated metabolic reprogramming in IL-37tg microglia.

results.result: In vivo neuroinflammatory processes are reduced in acutely inflammatory challenged mice after transgenic IL-37 expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is a summary conclusion supported by the comprehensive in vivo LPS challenge data (C64-C70) showing reduced microglial activation and inflammatory markers in IL-37tg mice.

results.result: Deleterious neuronal changes associated with acute inflammatory processes in the CNS are reduced in IL-37tg mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C153 is supported by the functional (LTP) and structural (dendritic spine) data (C71-C75) showing protection of neuronal function and morphology in IL-37tg mice after LPS challenge.

results.result: IL-37 expression directly in the CNS is responsible for reversing neuronal impairments after inflammatory challenge, independent of peripheral effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C155 is supported by the ex vivo slice experiments (C76-C78) demonstrating that local IL-37 expression in brain tissue is sufficient to prevent LPS-induced LTP impairments, providing critical mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Acute neuroinflammation, microglial activation, and deficits in plasticity and cognition induced by peripheral immune stimulation are attenuated or rescued by IL-37 (transgenic or recombinant), suggesting therapeutic potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C174 are summary conclusions supported by the comprehensive acute inflammation dataset including in vitro, in vivo, and recombinant IL-37 experiments (C48-C83). The convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches strongly supports these conclusions.

results.result: IL-37 overexpression in APP/PS1 mice results in higher plaque phagocytosis capacity, lower plaque burden, and smaller plaque size, suggesting that reduced inflammation leads to better Aβ clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C186 are supported by the plaque analysis and phagocytosis data (C90-C92), providing a mechanistic link between reduced inflammation and improved Aβ clearance in the chronic AD model.

results.result: IL-37 expression reduces neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in the APP/PS1 mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, with effects on synaptic plasticity, spine density, and amyloid-β plaque formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C205 are comprehensive summary conclusions supported by the extensive APP/PS1 dataset (C84-C102) including inflammation markers, plaque pathology, cognitive function, and synaptic measures. The convergent evidence strongly supports these integrative conclusions.

results.result: IL-37 alleviates acute and chronic neuroinflammatory conditions, providing basis for recombinant IL-37 as a potential therapeutic approach, with the IL-37tg mouse serving as a valuable model system.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C209 are overarching conclusions supported by the entire dataset spanning in vitro, acute in vivo, and chronic disease model experiments. The comprehensive evidence from multiple experimental paradigms and outcome measures strongly supports these final summary statements.

results.result: IL-37 most likely transmits its signals via microglia, with IL-18 receptor expression on microglial cells potentially responsible for IL-37 signal transduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C165 and C171 are mechanistic conclusions supported by the cell-type specific effects (C56, C126-C127) and RNA-seq data showing Il18r upregulation (C118). While the mechanism is not definitively proven, the evidence supports this as the most likely signaling pathway.

results.result: The lack of large differences in microglial gene expression profiles between WT and IL-37tg mice may be due to the timing of microglial isolation (3 hr after LPS injection).
results.evaluation: Claim C172 is speculative and acknowledges a limitation of the RNA-seq experiment. While the reasoning is plausible (transcriptional changes may precede protein changes), this remains an untested hypothesis that would require time-course experiments to verify.

results.result: The anti-inflammatory effect of IL-37 in the CNS may be a secondary effect due to reduction of peripheral inflammatory response.
results.evaluation: Claim C154 is contradicted by the ex vivo slice experiments (C76-C78, C155) which demonstrate direct CNS effects of IL-37 independent of peripheral immune responses. While peripheral effects may contribute, the evidence shows that local CNS expression is sufficient for neuroprotection.

results.result: Both intracellular and extracellular IL-37 signaling can reduce neuroinflammation during AD progression, with potential contributions from peripheral immune cell modulation, though the role of infiltrating immune cells remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C199 are largely speculative about mechanisms that were not directly tested in this study. While the dual signaling pathways of IL-37 are established in the literature (C146-C148), the specific contributions of each pathway and the role of peripheral immune cells in the APP/PS1 model remain uncertain and would require additional experiments to clarify.
